newsitem.title: UK: Russia, Peru under pressure in thin Brady market.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Peru under pressure in thin Brady market.

text.p: Russia slipped in the emerging debt market on Thursday while Peru, where negotiations continue to release hostages held at the Japanese ambassador's residence, was under continued pressure.
But traders said the market was very thin.
"People are a bit concerned that things in Russia may not be quite as they had looked," one Russian debt trader said.
Vneshekonombank dollar debt RUVNUSLNS=RR was bid 1/4 of a point lower at 76-3/8 cents in the dollar, closing in on lows of around 75 cents seen about a week ago.

"People are holding paper but they don't want to take on any more until things are clearer. There's a dribble of selling but no buyers and because the market is so thin the fall is exaggerated a bit," the trader said.
Some investors were given a fright by comments on Wednesday by Russian deputy finance minister Oleg Vyugin of a potential internal debt crisis.
However, analysts said the comments were a sensible warning rather than a prediction of an imminent crisis.
On the whole, the market remains very bullish about the outlook for the Russian economy, though analysts warn that serious hurdles remain.
A key issue in the short-term will be the International Monetary Fund's decision on when to release the November and December tranches of the loan.
Peruvian debt, which is on the way to being turned into Bradys, has come under strong pressure following the hostage crisis in Lima but there was no trading of the paper in London.

However, analysts said the problem throws unkind light on the country's social issues and has the potential to seriously undermine the popularity of President Alberto Fujimori and his commitment to economic reform.
ANZ analyst Jerome Booth said that while Fujimori could come out of the crisis with his popularity improved, if things go seriously wrong, there could be major problems for him.
Negotiations are continuing at the residence where leftist rebls are holding up to 484 hostages.
Fujimori's popularity, after six years in power, is already waning.
"He has destroyed democratic institutions in the country and as a result it is very vulnerable to big changes," Booth said.
Elsewhere there was very little activity.
Traders said there has been a little bit of bottom-fishing in Bulgaria.

Croatia has also been firming ahead of an expected credit rating though there is a fairly wide spread of views over how positive that rating will be, and some traders say an investment grade is not necessarily a certainty.
